\begin{abstract}
\noindent
Saudi commercial judgments are published with the appellate decision attached
to the judgment it reviews, giving \nPaired{} matched pairs of the same
dispute at two levels. \nNoReasonsShare{} per cent of appellate judgments give
no reasons of their own, affirming on the reasons below; whether a circuit
writes is not independent of what it decides, rising from
\nWroteAffirming{} per cent when it affirms to \nWroteReversing{} when it
reverses. Of appeals reaching the merits, \nDisturbedShare{} per cent disturb
the judgment. A logistic model on the \nModelN{} decided between
\nWindowFrom{} and \nWindowTo{} --- the window in which the record is mature
enough to read --- finds the procedural
share of a judgment's own citations the strongest protection against
disturbance (odds ratio \nOrProcedural{}) and one of \nHolmSurvivors{} terms
of eleven to survive correction for multiple testing. The judgment's citation
count and whether it wrote its own reasons predict nothing; its length
predicts weakly, and in the direction opposite to the one a reader would
guess.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} appellate review; judicial reason-giving; empirical
legal studies; court administration; Saudi Arabia

\section{Introduction}

An appeal is studied where appellate decisions are digitised, which in
practice has meant the United States and a handful of other common-law
systems. The second instance elsewhere is known largely through court
statistics: how many appeals were brought, how many succeeded. What the
appellate court actually wrote, set beside what the court below wrote in the
same dispute, is rarely available at scale in any jurisdiction, because the
two documents live in different places.

In Saudi Arabia they live in the same record. The Ministry of Justice
publishes commercial judgments in full text, and where a case went up, the
appellate decision is published attached to the judgment it reviews. That
yields \nPaired{} matched pairs --- the same dispute seen twice --- inside a
corpus of \nJudgments{} judgments, with a further \nAppealOnly{} appellate
decisions published alone. Nothing about the pairing was designed for
research; it is a by-product of how the publisher stores a case file. But it
removes the objection that defeats most comparisons between levels, which is
that the cases differ. Here they do not differ. They are the same cases.

Three things follow, and the first is about the institution rather than any
case. \nNoReasonsShare{} per cent of appellate judgments in this corpus give
no reasons of their own: they affirm on the reasons below, in the formula
\emph{mahmulan `ala asbabihi}. The second instance therefore adds its own
statement of reasoning to the public record in about one appeal in four.
Whether it does so is not independent of what it decides --- circuits wrote
their own reasons in \nWroteAffirming{} per cent of affirmances and
\nWroteReversing{} per cent of reversals --- which matters both as a finding
and as a constraint on the third result below.

Second, of the appeals that reached the merits, \nDisturbedShare{} per cent
disturbed the judgment: reversed it, replaced it with a fresh judgment, or
varied it. The rest affirmed. A further \nNotAdmittedShare{} per cent of all
appellate decisions never reached the merits at all, failing at the threshold,
and are excluded from that rate rather than counted as affirmances, because an
inadmissible objection says nothing about whether the judgment below was
sound.

Third, a logistic model asks what separates the judgments that were disturbed
from those that survived, using only what can be read from the first-instance
document. On the \nModelN{} decided between \nWindowFrom{} and \nWindowTo{},
the strongest protection is the procedural share of a judgment's own
statutory citations (odds ratio \nOrProcedural{}), one of only
\nHolmSurvivors{} terms of eleven to survive correction for multiple testing.
A judgment resting on the law of procedure is harder to disturb than
one resting on the law of obligations. The number of instruments it cites and
whether it wrote its own reasons predict nothing; its length predicts a
little, and longer judgments are disturbed slightly more often rather than
less.

Three methodological points are reported rather than assumed. The appellate
disposition is read from the operative part of the appellate document and
nowhere else, because an appellate recital narrates the history of the case
and a pattern applied to the whole document reads an earlier affirmance as
this court's ruling; the classifier was corrected four times against
hand-read samples before it was used. And the year in which a judgment was
given cannot be read across the whole span: a recent judgment appears here
with an appellate decision only if the appeal was both brought and decided
before the corpus was collected, so the disturbed rate falls from
\nModelBase{} per cent inside the mature window to almost nothing in the last
years of the span. The window is therefore an argument to the model rather
than a silent assumption, and the article reports the mature one.

The third is about the unit of analysis. Where a comparison is between two
levels of the same dispute, it is made over pairs and not over citations: citations
cluster inside judgments, and pooling them weights a dispute by how many
citations it happens to carry. That distinction is not cosmetic here. It
reverses the sign of one of this article's own earlier results, which
§\ref{sec:results} reports and withdraws.

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{What an appeal is for.} The economic account treats the appeal as
a device for correcting error at a cost, in which the party who lost has
private information about whether the decision was wrong and the system
relies on that information to select the cases worth reviewing.\footnote{%
Steven Shavell, ``The Appeals Process as a Means of Error Correction,''
\emph{Journal of Legal Studies} 24, no. 2 (1995): 379--426,
\url{https://doi.org/10.1086/467963}.} The account predicts a low disturbance rate among the appeals that are
brought, since litigants who know they were rightly beaten should not appeal;
what it does not predict is which surviving judgments differ from those
overturned, which is an empirical question this corpus can answer directly.

\paragraph{Measuring appellate outcomes.} The empirical literature on appeal
rates and outcomes is built largely on United States federal and state court
statistics, and is centrally concerned with who wins on appeal and why
plaintiffs do worse there than at trial.\footnote{%
Theodore Eisenberg, ``Appeal Rates and Outcomes in Tried and Nontried Cases:
Further Exploration of Anti-Plaintiff Appellate Outcomes,'' \emph{Journal of
Empirical Legal Studies} 1, no. 3 (2004): 659--88,
\url{https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1740-1461.2004.00019.x}.} That work reads
outcomes from docket records: the appellate decision is a category rather
than a text. This article reads the text, which permits questions a docket
cannot answer --- whether the appellate court reasoned at all, and what it
cited when it did --- at the price of being confined to what one publisher
publishes.

\paragraph{Reason-giving, and its limits.} That courts should give reasons is
among the least controversial propositions in procedural theory, and among
the least absolute in practice. Mathilde Cohen sets out the values that pull
against it --- efficiency, sincerity, and the risk of guidance a court is not
ready to give --- and shows common-law and civil-law systems converging on
similar compromises.\footnote{%
Mathilde Cohen, ``When Judges Have Reasons Not to Give Reasons: A Comparative
Law Approach,'' \emph{Washington and Lee Law Review} 72, no. 2 (2015): 483.} Affirming on the reasons below is one such compromise,
and a defensible one: reasons adopted are reasons given. Whether a court
adopts or writes is nevertheless observable, and the rate at which the second
instance writes has not been measured for this jurisdiction. It is measured
here.

\paragraph{The filters between a dispute and this dataset.} Two selection
problems bound everything below and cannot be removed by better extraction.
Cases that settle never produce a judgment, and settled disputes differ
systematically from tried ones.\footnote{%
George L. Priest and Benjamin Klein, ``The Selection of Disputes for
Litigation,'' \emph{Journal of Legal Studies} 13, no. 1 (1984): 1--55,
\url{https://doi.org/10.1086/467732}.} Of the judgments
given, publication is a second filter, and published and unpublished
decisions have been shown to differ in kind rather than merely in
number.\footnote{%
Peter Siegelman and John J. Donohue III, ``Studying the Iceberg from Its Tip:
A Comparison of Published and Unpublished Employment Discrimination Cases,''
\emph{Law \& Society Review} 24, no. 5 (1990): 1133--70,
\url{https://doi.org/10.2307/3053664}.} A third filter is specific to appeals and is
the more binding here: a judgment enters this analysis only if it was
appealed. Nothing in what follows describes judgments that no one challenged.

\paragraph{The jurisdiction.} Scholarship on Saudi law has been overwhelmingly
doctrinal and institutional, and until recently had little else to work with;
Frank Vogel's study remains the standard English-language treatment of the
courts, written before judgments were published at scale.\footnote{%
Frank E. Vogel, \emph{Islamic Law and Legal System: Studies of Saudi Arabia}
(Leiden: Brill, 2000).} The commercial courts whose
work this article measures were reorganised under a new law in 2020, and the
corpus is dominated by the years since.

\section{Data}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{A record that carries both levels}

The Ministry of Justice publishes Saudi commercial judgments in full text
through the interface its own portal uses. A published record holds the
judgment, and where the case was appealed it holds the appellate decision as
well, in a separate field of the same record. \nAppeals{} records carry an
appellate decision; \nPaired{} of those carry it beside the first-instance
judgment, and \nAppealOnly{} carry the appellate decision alone.

That storage decision is the whole of this article's data advantage, and it
was not made for research. It also caused a defect worth stating, because it
shows what the pairing does to naive processing: an earlier analysis of this
corpus segmented each record on its own headings, and where a record held two
judgments the segmentation ran from the reasons of the first into the
disposition of the second. Each document is now segmented separately.

\subsection{What the published record is}

The corpus holds \nJudgments{} judgments, overwhelmingly commercial and
concentrated in three cities and the last few Hijri years. Section
\ref{sec:threats} states the consequences. Two features of the published
fields matter for method rather than for interpretation. The interface
exposes \texttt{judgmentFacts}, \texttt{judgmentReasons} and
\texttt{judgmentRuling}, which are null in every record, so the structure of a
judgment must be read from its text. And it exposes \texttt{isAppeal}, which
is present, well-typed, and false on every record --- including every record
that carries an appellate decision. First instance and appeal are separated
here by the fields that hold the text, not by the flag provided for the
purpose.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Reading the appellate disposition}

The disposition is read from the operative part of the appellate document and
from nowhere else. An appellate recital routinely narrates the history of the
case, including earlier affirmances, so a pattern applied to the whole
document reports an old affirmance as this court's ruling. The operative part
is located by the markers Saudi circuits use to introduce it, and only the
text after the last such marker is classified; where the operative part
quotes the judgment below --- which it usually does, at length --- the quoted
disposition is cut away before classification, and the label is whichever
disposition the court states first.

Dispositions are classified as affirmed, reversed, replaced by a fresh
judgment, varied, not admitted, disposed of on another ground, or unclear.
Nothing is forced: a document whose operative part cannot be located, or
whose disposition matches none of these, is unclear and is reported as such.

The classifier was corrected four times, each time against a hand-read
sample rather than by inspection. The operative part is fully vowelled in a
few hundred judgments and a plain-script pattern missed all of them; a
refusal of a request for arbitration is not an inadmissible appeal; the
window swallowed the quoted judgment below; and a fixed order of tests read
\emph{affirming a judgment that had reversed an administrative decision} as
a reversal. On a random sample of twenty classifications read after the last
correction, none was wrong.

\subsection{Whether the appeal reasoned}

Saudi judgments carry their own structure --- \emph{al-waqa'i}, then
\emph{al-asbab}, then the operative part --- and an appellate document is
counted as having reasoned when that structure is present within it. This is
a count of whether the second instance put its own reasoning on the record,
not a judgment about quality: a circuit affirming on the reasons below has
given reasons by adoption.

\subsection{Modelling disturbance}

The model is a logistic regression of disturbance on features of the
first-instance judgment. Disturbed means reversed, replaced or varied;
affirmed means affirmed. Appeals that never reached the merits are excluded
rather than coded as affirmances.

Every feature is read from the first-instance document alone: the city, the
Hijri year, the length of the text, the number of statutory citations, the
number of distinct instruments cited, the procedural share of those
citations, whether the judgment carried its own reasons under the headings,
whether its operative part disposed of the case on the merits rather than on
a preliminary point, and whether a preliminary defence was raised in it. A
model that saw the appellate text would be predicting the outcome from
itself.

The fit is by iteratively reweighted least squares, written out rather than
imported: the replication guide promises that the analysis runs with no
third-party package, and a reviewer running the pipeline should not discover
otherwise because one script wanted a matrix inverse.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{What appeals do}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Appellate dispositions across \nAppeals{} published appellate
decisions.}
\label{tab:outcomes}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Disposition & Judgments & Share \\
\midrule
Affirmed                       & \nAffirmed{}     & \nAffirmedShare{}\% \\
Reversed                       & \nReversed{}     & \nReversedShare{}\% \\
Replaced by a fresh judgment   & \nSubstituted{}  & \nSubstitutedShare{}\% \\
Varied                         & \nVaried{}       & --- \\
Not admitted                   & \nNotAdmitted{}  & \nNotAdmittedShare{}\% \\
Disposed of on another ground  & \nOtherDisposition{} & \nOtherShare{}\% \\
Unclear                        & \nUnclearOutcome{}   & \nUnclearShare{}\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:outcomes} gives the dispositions. \nDecidedOnMerits{}
decisions reached the merits, and \nDisturbedShare{} per cent of those
disturbed the judgment below. The rate is low, as the error-correction
account predicts of appeals that are brought at all, and the striking figure
beside it is the \nNotAdmittedShare{} per cent that failed at the threshold:
about one appellate decision in seven never reached the question the appellant
wanted answered.

\subsection{Reason-giving at the second instance}

\nOwnReasons{} appellate judgments --- \nOwnReasonsShare{} per cent --- carry
reasons of their own. The remaining \nNoReasonsShare{} per cent affirm or
dispose on the reasons below.

Whether a circuit writes is not independent of what it decides. It wrote in
\nWroteAffirming{} per cent of affirmances, \nWroteReversing{} per cent of
reversals, \nWroteSubstituting{} per cent where it replaced the judgment with
its own, and \nWroteNotAdmitting{} per cent where the appeal failed at the
threshold. A circuit that leaves the judgment standing mostly adopts the
reasoning below; a circuit that disturbs it mostly explains itself. That is
what one would want of an appellate court, and it is also what makes the
comparison in the next subsection a biased sample of appeals rather than a
sample of appeals.

\subsection{Reasoning compared, where both levels reasoned}

Both levels reasoned in \nBothReasoned{} pairs, \nBothReasonedShare{} per
cent of the pairs. Pooled over citations, the appellate reasons look more
procedural than the reasons below --- \nAppealProcedural{} per cent against
\nFirstProcedural{} --- and drawn from a narrower set of instruments,
\nAppealInstruments{} distinct instruments against \nFirstInstruments{}.

That figure is computed on the wrong unit, and it does not survive being put
on the right one. Citations are not independent draws: they cluster inside
judgments, so pooling them weights a pair by how many citations it happens to
carry, and a few citation-heavy appellate documents can carry the average.
Table~\ref{tab:paired} runs the same comparison over pairs. Each of the
\nPairsTested{} pairs in which both levels cite a matched instrument
contributes one number --- the procedural share of the appellate reasons minus
the procedural share of the reasons below --- and the null that the levels do
not differ is tested by flipping the sign of that number at random, which is
the exact randomisation test for paired data and assumes nothing about its
distribution.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{The same comparison over pairs rather than over citations. A negative
difference means the appellate reasons are less procedural than the reasons
below. Two-sided $p$ by sign-flip permutation.}
\label{tab:paired}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Pairs where both levels cited & Pairs & Mean difference & $p$ \\
\midrule
All                      & \nPairsTested{}    & \nDiffAll{}       & \nPDiffAll{} \\
The appeal affirmed      & \nPairsAffirmed{}  & \nDiffAffirmed{}  & \nPDiffAffirmed{} \\
The appeal disturbed     & \nPairsDisturbed{} & \nDiffDisturbed{} & \nPDiffDisturbed{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The sign reverses. Over all pairs the mean paired difference is
\nDiffAll{} percentage points --- the appellate reasons are, if anything,
\emph{less} procedural than the reasons below --- and it does not reach
significance ($p$ = \nPDiffAll{}). Split by outcome, the affirmances that
dominate the pooled figure show nothing at all (\nDiffAffirmed{} points, $p$ =
\nPDiffAffirmed{}, on \nPairsAffirmed{} pairs). The difference lives in the
\nPairsDisturbed{} pairs where the appeal disturbed the judgment:
\nDiffDisturbed{} points, $p$ = \nPDiffDisturbed{}. A circuit that overturns
reaches for substantive law more than the judgment it overturned did.

Two things follow, and the first is a withdrawal. On the unit at which the
claim is actually made, appellate reasons are not more procedural than the
reasons below; the pooled statement was an artefact of weighting pairs by
their citation counts, and it is withdrawn rather than qualified. The second
is that the surviving difference is reported with the same discipline applied
to it: three tests appear in Table~\ref{tab:paired}, and $p$ =
\nPDiffDisturbed{} would not survive correction for three any more than a
model term at that level survives correction for eleven. It is reported as a
signal that the strata differ, not as an established difference.

\subsection{What predicts disturbance}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Logistic regression of disturbance on features of the first-instance
judgment, \nWindowFrom{}--\nWindowTo{}. \nModelN{} judgments, base rate
\nModelBase{} per cent.}
\label{tab:model}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Feature of the judgment below & Odds ratio & $p$ & Holm $p$ \\
\midrule
Procedural share of its citations & \nOrProcedural{} & \nPProcedural{} & \nHolmProcedural{} \\
Hijri year                        & \nOrYear{}       & \nPYear{}       & \nHolmYear{} \\
Dammam                            & \nOrDammam{}     & \nPDammam{}     & \nHolmDammam{} \\
Riyadh                            & \nOrRiyadh{}     & \nPRiyadh{}     & \nHolmRiyadh{} \\
Jeddah                            & \nOrJeddah{}     & \nPJeddah{}     & \nHolmJeddah{} \\
Disposed on the merits            & \nOrMerits{}     & \nPMerits{}     & \nHolmMerits{} \\
Preliminary defence raised        & \nOrDefence{}    & \nPDefence{}    & \nHolmDefence{} \\
Wrote its own reasons             & \nOrReasons{}    & \nPReasons{}    & \nHolmReasons{} \\
Length (log characters)           & \nOrLength{}     & \nPLength{}     & \nHolmLength{} \\
Number of citations               & \nOrCitations{}  & \nPCitations{}  & \nHolmCitations{} \\
Distinct instruments cited        & \nOrInstruments{} & \nPInstruments{} & \nHolmInstruments{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Eleven coefficients are tested at once, so the table carries a Holm-adjusted
$p$ beside the raw one, and the text below treats as established only the
\nHolmSurvivors{} terms that survive it.

The strongest coefficient in Table~\ref{tab:model} is the procedural share of
a judgment's own citations, at \nOrProcedural{} (Holm $p$ =
\nHolmProcedural{}). A judgment whose statutory authority is procedural is
markedly harder to disturb than one resting on the law of obligations,
controlling for whether it decided the merits at all. The other two survivors
are the Hijri year, which is reported only inside the mature window for the
reason given in §\ref{sec:threats}, and one city: Dammam's judgments are
disturbed more often than the other cities' at \nOrDammam{} (Holm $p$ =
\nHolmDammam{}), which this article records and does not explain.

Three terms are worth as much as the coefficients because they are flat on
every reading of the table. The number of statutory citations in a judgment
(\nOrCitations{}), the number of distinct instruments it cites
(\nOrInstruments{}), and whether it wrote its own reasons under the headings
(\nOrReasons{}) do not predict whether it survives. A heavily cited judgment
is not a safer judgment.

Two terms sit between the two groups and are reported rather than relied on.
Deciding the merits is protective at \nOrMerits{} and length is mildly
aggravating at \nOrLength{}; each is significant on the raw $p$
(\nPMerits{} and \nPLength{}) and neither survives correction
(\nHolmMerits{} and \nHolmLength{}). Which way length points is worth
recording even so, because it is not the direction a reader would guess:
longer judgments are disturbed slightly more often, not less. Nothing in this
model supports the idea that a judgment protects itself by being long.

\section{Threats to validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{Only appealed judgments are here.} A judgment enters this analysis
because someone challenged it. Nothing here describes the judgments no one
appealed, which are the great majority, and the disturbance rate is a rate
among appeals rather than an error rate among judgments.

\paragraph{Recent judgments are censored, which is why the window is an
argument.} A judgment appears with an appellate decision only if the appeal
was brought and decided before the corpus was collected. For the most recent
years that selects the fastest appeals. The measured disturbance rate rises
through the mature years and then collapses in the last two, which is a fact
about the collection date and not about the courts. The model is therefore
reported on \nWindowFrom{}--\nWindowTo{}, and the whole span is kept as the
comparison that shows why.

\paragraph{Who writes reasons is not random, and the comparison inherits it.}
The reasoning comparison uses the \nBothReasonedShare{} per cent of pairs
where both levels reasoned, and reasoning goes with disturbing: a circuit that
disturbs a judgment writes its own reasons far more often than one that
affirms. Every statement about appellate reasoning in this article is
therefore a statement about that minority of appeals, selected by their
outcome, and not about appeals in general.

\paragraph{Eleven terms, three strata, one corpus.} Testing many things on one
body of data produces small $p$-values on its own. Both the model and the
paired comparison are reported with that in mind: Table~\ref{tab:model}
carries the Holm-adjusted $p$ and only \nHolmSurvivors{} of its eleven terms
are relied on, and the difference in Table~\ref{tab:paired} is reported as a
signal rather than an established result for the same reason. Where an earlier
version of this analysis pooled citations instead of pairs, the correction
reversed a sign, and the withdrawal is recorded in §\ref{sec:results} rather
than removed from it.

\paragraph{The corpus is what the Ministry publishes.} It is overwhelmingly
commercial and urban. Cases that settle produce no judgment at all, and
published and unpublished decisions differ. Every rate here is a rate within
the published record.

\paragraph{The classifier is lexical.} The disposition is read from operative
language, validated by hand, and left unclear rather than guessed where the
language does not decide it; \nUnclearShare{} per cent of appellate decisions
are unclear and are excluded from the rates that depend on the disposition.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The finding with the widest reach is the one that requires no model. In about
three appellate decisions in four, the second instance adds no reasoning of
its own to the public record. That is lawful, it is efficient, and on the
reason-giving literature's own account it is defensible: reasons adopted are
reasons given. But it has a consequence for anyone outside the case. A
practitioner who wants to know what an appellate court thinks of an argument
will find, in three files out of four, only that it agreed with someone else;
and a researcher measuring appellate reasoning is measuring a minority of
appeals selected by their outcome. A court system that publishes its
judgments has decided that its reasoning is a public good. The rate at which
the second instance actually supplies it is therefore a measurable feature of
that policy, and it can be reported alongside clearance rates and disposal
times without anyone having to read a judgment.

The model's central coefficient joins this article to the question its
predecessor asked. Measuring what Saudi courts cite shows an applied law that
is overwhelmingly procedural. Measuring what survives appeal shows why that
may be self-reinforcing: the procedural share of a judgment's own citations
is the strongest protection against disturbance in this model. A judgment
grounded in the law of procedure is harder to overturn than one grounded in
the law of obligations. Whether that is because procedural questions have
determinate answers, or because appellate circuits are readier to substitute
their own view on substance, this data cannot say --- but the incentive it
describes points one way.

The nulls deserve their own sentence. Citation count, the breadth of
authority cited, and whether the court below wrote its own reasons do not
predict survival, and length predicts it only weakly and in the wrong
direction for any account on which thoroughness protects. If judicial training
or performance measurement rewards the appearance of thoroughness --- a long
judgment, a wall of citations --- it is rewarding something this record does
not connect to outcomes.

\section{Conclusion}

Saudi commercial judgments are published with the appellate decision inside
the record of the judgment it reviews. That accident of storage yields
\nPaired{} matched pairs and answers questions dockets cannot: not only how
often appeals succeed, but whether the second instance explains itself, and
what distinguishes the judgments it lets stand.

It explains itself in about one appeal in four, and more often when it
disturbs than when it affirms. \nDisturbedShare{} per cent of appeals that
reach the merits disturb the judgment. And the feature of a judgment that
best protects it is not its length or the weight of authority it cites, but
that its authority is procedural.

\section*{Availability of data and code}

The corpus, the extraction and classification code, the model, and the
scripts that generate every number in this article are public.\footnote{%
\ifanon
Repository withheld for anonymous review: its address names the author. It
holds the corpus, the analysis code and the replication guide, and will be
cited in full in the accepted version.
\else
Repository: \url{https://github.com/Abdullah-m7/saudi-legal-corpus-ai}.
\fi
Every measurement here is generated into a file of macros by
\texttt{make\_numbers.py} and typeset from it; a check refuses to build a
manuscript that types one by hand.} Judgments are reproduced as the Ministry
publishes them, with parties' names masked at source and a further redaction
pass over identifiers the publisher's masking missed.

\section*{Use of AI tools}

The analysis code and drafts of this manuscript were produced with the
assistance of a large language model (Anthropic's Claude) working under the
author's direction. The author designed the study, framed every question,
verified each result against the corpus, and is responsible for the content.
No measurement in this article is produced by a language model: every number
is computed by the deposited code from the deposited data.
